If you don't already use custom router firmware, like OpenWRT or DD-WRT, you should.

Insecure routers are an often overlooked, yet easily penetrable way into your home network. Once inside your network, it becomes trivial to access other devices.. laptops, phones, any other wifi/network-accessible device.

In no particular order:

  1. Most routers have a short shelf life and don't offer firmware updates for very long past the date of sale - that leaves you with security holes that are easily exploited by bad guys trolling the neighborhood, or, if you're a person of interest - your adversary can effortlessly collect your daily web activities, account credentials.. and when major exploits are released, the open source router firmwares are among the first to get patched.

  2. Many of them offer little-to-no security! A network firewall is absolutely integral, many IOT devices (TVs, fridges, tons of other gadgets that shouldn't have web access but do..) get owned by very basic port scans - bad guys run scanners on entire IP blocks looking for specific ports commonly used by IOT garbage - if you don't have defenses to prevent such things, they can enter your home network through such devices.

  3. You can set up VLANS / network segmentation. This is an 'advanced' setup, but a noob could absolutely achieve it with a little effort. VLANs would allow you to create a "wall" between untrusted devices. Put that smart TV on its own network - leave your laptop on another. Without network isolation, some devices are programmed to send "chatter" or look for other devices.. from that, they collect data about your home and phone home to the mothership. Some ISP routers allow you to do isolation, too, but plug-n-play will typically break. VLANs are great because, should one of your shitty IOT devices get hacked, the intruder is confined inside the walls of that VLAN and providing you set them up correctly, they cannot reach into other VLANs or other parts of your network.

  4. Network-wide adblocking - you can add an adblocker at the network level. So any device in your home can browse the web the way it's supposed to be, free of trackers and advertising!

  5. Plugins/increased customizability - There's a ton of cool things you can do that you probably never even thought of.

  6. VPN your entire network.. if you're that paranoid. Would not recommend banking on a VPN (unless you run your own VPN and really know what you're doing), though.

  7. NAS support - If you have a USB-capable router

  8. Custom DNS - Your ISP undoubtedly sells your browsing history. Ditch their defaults (which are often locked in ISP-owned routers) and use something like OpenNIC or DNSCrypt, instead

Just a few examples. Do your own research, don't take my word for it!

But at least consider what kind of doors you leave open.

Others have said pfSense and it's a good recommendation - for hardware use non-US based, non-China fabbed hardware like PC Engines for all the glow in the dark reasons frequently mentioned here.

Keep Wireless separate for performance reasons - Ubiquiti is good for price/performance/support and while WiFi 6/WPA 3 isn't ready yet the current hardware generation will be good for a few years. If you want the full glow in the dark resistant experience use another small hardware device and pfSense again.

For pfSense boxes turn on features carefully and question why you need the feature in the first place. An IDS/IPS is wonderful but has huge performance overhead and is blind to most network traffic e..g HTTPS.

Don't do VLANs it's very technical for most and additional overhead for small reward - use the extra port(s) on the pfSense route and split the network using addressing - you can use a common switch behind it with no setup, again Ubiquiti is good and I see others have recommended it so upvoats for them.

For the technical - use /27 for major functions and /64 for IPv6 because you're doing dual stack, right? As an example one subnet for workstations, one subnet for servers, one subnet for IoT and one for wireless. The pfSense firewall blocks comms between all and only allow the minimum required. Outbound can be controlled to only allow traffic to pfSense proxies or as you would like.

Use DNSCrypt, this is probably the most serious lesson. Glow in the darks love DNS, it's "low" bandwidth and easy to rewrite so it's common to see man-in-the-middle enforcement actions that block/redirect domains. Use a managed or free provider, Cisco Umbrella are too corporate and block too many things you have to override.

You'll bypass a lot of content blocks with DNSCrypt and there are mobile clients that help with censorship when you're roaming, DNS Cloak is good for iOS as an example. You can choose your content blocks rather than having them shoved down your throat by the wireless/ISP and/or glowies.

Then block all outbound DNS other than your DNSCrypt server, go "dark" to the glowies! Block all common outbound signalling if you really want e.g. Microsoft/Apple/Google telemetry, NTP, you name it. Go as dark as you need to be because DNS is a fundamental protocol and enfocring it to your tastes gives you as much control as possible.

The BSI did a really good writeup on Windows telemetry as an example, the NSA has some good materials on keeping your home network secure. These are frenemies so I don't link directly and use other sources you trust to compare recommendations.

Source: me, have done all this stuff plus a lot more...

Avoid Cloudflare at all costs, there are many alternatives even for their CDN/DDoS services, use Quad9 if you have to but really there are better alternatives that use DNSCrypt.

When it comes to attaching random stuff to your network, so long as you understand the risks and can control them go for it!
You can also just null route packets for untrusted devices that are trying to phone home.

VPNs are very easy to defeat. Do not let them lull you into a false sense of security. Everything you do online should be done with the assumption that other people can see what you are doing. It's really the only safe way to use the internet.
